angle: The CEO asked a market question. I built an agent that answered it from our CRM data in 10 minutes
post_first_line: 10 minutes. One agent. One CEO question answered.
linkedin_post:
10 minutes. One agent. One CEO question answered.

Jeff Kirchick got a market question that most teams would turn into a week-long analysis project.

The CEO pointed out that the company sells an ICHRA, a healthcare benefit that works better in some states than others. Some states are friendlier to it than others.

So Jeff built an agent on top of the company's HubSpot data. It compared the number of quotes being run in each state against how friendly that market is to the product.

The output showed where the company is underinvesting in its market.

That matters right now because the team is hiring. Jeff now has a data-backed sense of where a new person should sit.

The whole thing took about 10 minutes.

The CRM data was already there. The question was already clear. What changed is how fast one person can connect the two.

What's the last question you answered by gut instead of data?

takeaways: A good market question plus data you already own can become an agent in minutes.
Comparing effort (quotes run) against opportunity (market friendliness) exposes where you are underinvesting.
Tie the analysis to a live decision, like where to place a new hire, so it gets used.
lesson.exercise: Pick one question leadership has asked this quarter. Write down the two data points that would answer it, then build a quick agent over your CRM to compare them.

angle: I could automate all my coaching. Here's why I walked it back.
post_first_line: Neema Zarrabian has 30 to 50 coaching rules.
linkedin_post:
Neema Zarrabian has 30 to 50 coaching rules.

That's the setup for why Neema stopped short of automating all of it.

Neema could automate every bit of coaching: 30, 40, 50 rules, 7 customer stories, and all the points reps should hit on a call.

For a month, Neema built Notion docs for each rep covering the questions they couldn't answer, then sent them over in Slack.

Then came the shift. Neema still does some of that, but now goes through it live with the rep.

Watching a call together. Taking notes. Hearing how a rep says things. Asking why they went one direction and not another.

The findings also go into one-on-one docs, along with a simple check: do you feel good about this?

The takeaway from Neema: there is something human about coaching. Reps get held accountable and become coachable through live conversation, not a doc dropped in Slack.

Automation can handle the rules. The conversation about a real deal is what builds the rep.

What part of coaching have you refused to automate?

lesson.title: Why live coaching beats automated coaching
takeaways: Rules and customer stories can be documented, but they don't replace talking through a real deal with a rep.
Watching a call together shows how a rep says things and why they chose one direction over another.
One-on-one docs plus a check on how the rep feels keep coaching accountable and human.

angle: How a seller with no engineering background built a working Salesforce-to-Slack-to-Gmail bot from one Claude Code session
post_first_line: 45 minutes to run one simple Salesforce report.
linkedin_post:
45 minutes to run one simple Salesforce report.

That was Matt Stinson's starting point, and three months later Matt had a working bot built in a single Claude Code session.

Matt described exactly what the bot should do, then planned out the infrastructure with Claude Code. Here's how the pieces fit together:

1. Custom Apex class code in Salesforce posts a webhook that acts as the trigger.
2. Railway hosts the interface that monitors that trigger.
3. The trigger pushes to a Slack bot, where the end user interacts with it.
4. Gmail handles the final mile, and the result flows back into Salesforce.

Three months earlier, Matt didn't know what Apex class code was and barely knew how to run customized reports in Salesforce.

Matt's take: the only limit now is having a good idea.

What would you build if setup stopped being the barrier?

takeaways: You don't need to know the technical terms up front. Describe exactly what you want and plan the infrastructure from there.
A simple chain can carry a whole workflow: a Salesforce trigger, a hosted monitor, a Slack interface, Gmail, and back into Salesforce.
Matt didn't know what Apex class code was three months earlier, so the limit is the idea, not the background.

angle: Ask AI what you're not thinking about. Start with one micro problem.
post_first_line: Matt Stinson asked Claude what Matt wasn't thinking about.
linkedin_post:
Matt Stinson asked Claude what Matt wasn't thinking about.

That one question turned a pile of raw data into a repeatable workflow.

Matt hadn't connected any AI tool to Salesforce yet. So Matt downloaded rep data, conversion data, and funnel data, then opened a chat with Claude Code.

The prompt was simple: here are the things Matt is thinking about, now tell Matt something new.

They went back and forth. Somewhere in that loop, a pattern showed up. It could be bundled into a skill or a flow.

Now the plan is to run the same process every week before one-on-ones.

Matt's takeaway: start with a specific micro problem, then scale from there. It's a good process to follow when deciding where to build.

No big architecture plan. No full integration first. Just one small problem and a conversation.

What's your one micro problem to start with?
